slides.0.title: Raw materials and methods of sparkling wine
slides.0.subtitle: Where the second fermentation happens decides style and cost
slides.1.title: Base wine and climate
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Why cool climates
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Sparkling wine needs high-acid, low-alcohol, neutral base wine: the second fermentation adds roughly another 1–1.5% alcohol, and acidity carries the freshness of the bubbles. Hence top regions tend to be cool or marginal (Champagne, England, Tasmania)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Approaches in warm regions
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Warm regions keep acidity through early picking, altitude or cool coastal sites (e.g. higher Penedès for Cava, high-altitude sparkling in Argentina’s Uco), adding acid if needed
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Choice of varieties
slides.1.highlights.2.content: The traditional method mostly uses Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, with local varieties elsewhere (Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada in Cava, Chenin Blanc in the Loire). Aromatic sparkling wines choose expressive varieties (Glera, Moscato)
slides.1.content: Quality sparkling wine starts with a high-acid base wine that is not pleasant on its own.
slides.2.title: The main methods
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Traditional method
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Second fermentation, lees ageing, riddling, disgorgement and dosage all in the same bottle; the most expensive, giving fine bubbles and autolytic character (Champagne, Cava, Franciacorta, Crémant)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Transfer method
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Second fermentation and ageing in bottle, but the wine is emptied into a pressurised tank, filtered and rebottled instead of riddling; used for unusual bottle sizes, with flavour close to the traditional method
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Tank method (Charmat)
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Second fermentation in a sealed tank, then filtration and bottling; quick and cheap, preserving primary fruit: the method for Prosecco and most Sekt
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Ancestral and Asti methods
slides.2.highlights.3.content: The ancestral method bottles wine before the first fermentation finishes so it completes in bottle (Gaillac, Limoux, pét-nat); the Asti method has a single fermentation in a pressurised tank, stopped by chilling to keep sweetness and low alcohol
slides.2.content: A D4 staple: for each method, say where the second fermentation happens, whether there is riddling, and the consequences for style and cost.
slides.3.title: Autolysis, dosage and pressure
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Lees ageing and autolysis
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Dead yeast cells break down and release compounds that give bread, brioche and biscuit notes and finer bubbles with a smoother texture; the longer on the lees, the stronger the autolytic character (a tendency)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Dosage and sweetness
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Liqueur d’expédition is added after disgorgement; EU sweetness terms run from Brut Nature (<3 g/L) to Doux (>50 g/L). Dosage balances acidity, shapes texture and influences post-disgorgement ageing
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Pressure and style
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Fully sparkling wines (spumante, mousseux) are about 5–6 bar; semi-sparkling (frizzante, pétillant) about 1–2.5 bar. Franciacorta Satèn is deliberately under 5 bar for a softer mousse
slides.3.content: Blind-tasting clue: autolytic notes → traditional method with longer ageing; bright fruit without autolysis → usually tank method.
slides.4.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Why are top sparkling-wine regions usually cool?
A. They need high-acid, low-alcohol base wine
B. Cool regions pay less tax
C. MLF only works in the cool
D. Cool regions need no yeast
The second fermentation adds more alcohol.
Which method does Prosecco mainly use?
A. Transfer method
B. Tank method (Charmat)
C. Traditional method
D. Ancestral method
The tank method keeps Glera’s primary fruit.
What characterises the Asti method?
A. Long lees ageing is required
B. Riddling and disgorgement are required
C. A single fermentation stopped by chilling to keep sweetness
D. Both fermentations in bottle
Hence low alcohol and sweetness.
How does Franciacorta Satèn differ most from standard sparkling wine?
A. It must be sweet
B. It uses the tank method
C. It is a red sparkling wine
D. Pressure under 5 bar, softer mousse
Satèn uses white grapes only.
